column11: types
Imports point inward, toward stability, and form no cycle, direct or through a chain of modules.
The inner layer declares, in its own words, the contracts it needs; the outer layer implements them.
The domain imports only itself and the shared kernel: no framework, no input or output, no vendor library, however pure.
Each layer, module and unit has one reason to change.
Every datum and every piece of state lives in one place; everything else reads it or derives from it.
A feature never imports another feature.
A module is reached from outside only through its surface, and the surface is curated: it offers what a caller may couple to and nothing else.
An external shape — a response, a row, a message, a file format — is mapped to the inner model at the edge, in both directions.
Input and output, network, storage, clock, randomness and processes live in adapters.
Concrete implementations are chosen and wired in one known place, the composition root.
Where one operation reads and another writes, the read path and the write path never import each other.
Code lives in the layer that owns its reason to change, beside its consumer when they share that reason, and lifts to the nearest common level only when a second consumer appears.
A value with distinct stages is a union keyed by its state, not a bag of optional fields and flags that allows combinations no stage has.
A caught error is handled, rethrown, or mapped to a typed error.
Every rule whose Check names a role is held by a tool of that role in the project's check, configured to fail on a violation.
A contract is shaped by the role that uses it: a reader sees only reads, a writer only writes, and no caller receives an operation it has no reason to call.
Input from outside the program — a request, a response, a file, the environment — is parsed once, at the edge, into a known type.
A new kind of thing — a vendor, a command, a format, a rule — is added as a new member and its registration, without editing the code that handles the other kinds.
Across bounded contexts, duplication is the default and sharing the exception.
A value object is built only through the function that checks its invariant, so a value that exists is valid.

Where the program owns the data it changes, every change goes through its aggregate's root, which keeps the aggregate consistent; an aggregate stays small, and a child with a life of its own becomes an aggregate referenced by identifier.
A program's source is laid out by concern in the folders of the top-level tree, and in no other top-level folder.
`root/` is imported only by entry files and by the delivery layer's own wiring.
No code imports an entrypoint.
`kernel/` imports only itself.
`libs/` imports no application code — no feature, `kernel/`, `shared/`, `contracts/`, `adapters/` or `root/` — and knows nothing of the repository that uses it.
`shared/` imports no feature and not `root/`.
A shared piece with business meaning goes to `kernel/`; one without goes to `shared/`; one that would make sense in any program goes to `libs/`.
Composition across features lives in the delivery unit that needs it, which assembles features through their surfaces.
A protocol two artifacts of one repository speak — the messages an embedded frame and its host exchange — lives in `shared/<protocol>/`, imported by both.
A file a tool produces carries `.gen` in its name or sits in a folder named `*.gen/`, and is never edited by hand; a change goes to its source, and the file is regenerated.
A feature is laid out as `domain/`, `adapters/<system>/` and `app/` with the role folders of the tree, and a surface at its root.

A data port is a repository per aggregate, one file per side: `repositories/queries/<aggregate>.repository` for reads and `repositories/commands/<aggregate>.repository` for writes, each declaring its operations' parameters and results.
A domain use-case exists only when its operation carries business logic.
A contract — a port, its parameters and results — imports no vendor, no adapter, no feature other than its own, and no other contract's internals.
An adapter imports its contracts, `kernel/` and `libs/`, and never a feature's application layer, the delivery layer or another adapter.
A feature that needs an answer from another declares a contract in its own words and receives an input built for it; composition implements the contract through the other feature's surface.
Outside a folder, a caller imports only its surface.
A layer folder — `domain/`, `app/`, `adapters/`, `src/`, `features/`, `libs/` — has no surface and is never an import target.
A surface re-exports by name what callers may use: no declaration, no logic, no re-export of everything.
A feature's surface offers its operations and its presentation — use-cases, binding units, entities, widgets — and never its mechanisms: repositories, mappers, wire types, cache keys.
A contract belongs to the feature that needs it.
An adapter implements, over one external system, every contract of its owner that system serves; it lives beside its contracts' owner.
An adapter with injected dependencies is built by a factory function; a stateless adapter may be a module object.
A port for an effect — clock, file system, processes, network — is a contract placed like any other, its real implementation is an adapter, and only a composition root chooses the real one.
A vendor client without application knowledge, and any pure project-agnostic helper, lives in `libs/<system>/`.
A delivery unit that serves one feature lives in that feature's `app/`, where the entry surface allows it; one that composes several lives in the delivery layer or in `composition/`.
A delivery unit — a screen, a command, a handler, a tool function — parses its input, calls a use-case or a binding unit, and presents the result.
A folder is named for its purpose, or by a role of the vocabulary of the project's active blocks.
A folder holds one purpose, said in one phrase without "and".
Files of one kind that arrive one at a time — one per vendor, command, rule or section — live in a folder named for the member in the plural, and nothing else lives there.
A file carries its role's suffix, whatever its folder: `entities/chat.entity`.
A YAML file ends in `.yaml`, never `.yml`.
A name says what a thing is for: intention-revealing, pronounceable, searchable, with no abbreviation that is not already a term of the domain and no noise word.
Names follow the business's own words, from the glossary of `PROJECT.md`: `cancelOrder`, not `updateRecord`.
One concept has one word across the program, and one word names one concept: not `fetch`, `load` and `get` for the same act.
No name is only an empty word — `data`, `result`, `temp`, `info`, `item`, `value`, `obj`, `arr`, `stuff`, `thing` — as a variable, a parameter or a destructured field.
A function is named by a concrete verb and its object, never an empty verb alone: `handle`, `process`, `manage`, `do`, `run`, `execute`, `get`, `set`, `update`.
A collection is named in the plural and one of its items in the singular, destructured names included.
An event is named for what happened, in the past tense: `OrderPlaced`, not `PlaceOrder`.
A domain name names the concept, never the vendor or the storage behind it: `UserRecord`, not `UserMongoDocument`.
A value with a unit carries the unit in its name: `timeoutMs`, `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`, `sizeBytes`.
A file holds one semantic unit and is named after it; unrelated exports go to their own files.
A boolean variable, parameter or predicate starts with `is`, `has`, `can`, `should` or `did`.
Every argument past the first is named: the language's options record or keyword-only parameters.
A function does one thing, at one level of abstraction.
A function holds at most 100 lines, a file at most 500, and a function's cognitive complexity is at most 10.
Failure paths leave first, through guard clauses, so the main path stays at the top level of indentation.
A module hides much behind a small interface.
A function's output depends only on its input.
A longer, obvious form beats a terse, obscure one.
A comment states a constraint, a workaround or a decision the code cannot show.
Interface documentation is written only for a public interface whose use is not obvious from its names and types.
A to-do comment names its issue: `TODO(#<issue>)`.
Code is never commented out; it is deleted.
No unused file, dependency, export, parameter, variable or branch.
Shipped code writes no debug output and stops at no breakpoint; diagnostics go through the logging port.
Silencing a check — a lint rule, a type error, a mutant, a deliberately ignored error — carries its reason beside it.
Internal code spells absence with one value, which the language block names.
An expected failure is typed, carries a stable code `<MODULE>_<ENTITY>_<KIND>` and details that say what to do, and belongs to the contract that can fail.
A mapped error keeps its cause.
Defects travel to the boundary.
Only a transient failure — a timeout, a dropped connection, a rate limit — is retried, with backoff and a limit.
An error library gives every error a stable code, its cause and structured details, and a guard that recognises its errors by code.
A schema over a domain type or enum derives its values from it and is checked by type against what it produces.
A type guard checks every property of the type it claims.
An entity's identifier is a type of its own, branded by its entity, so an order's identifier cannot be passed where a user's is expected.
A type lives beside the unit whose signature introduces it, and every other unit imports it from there.
Values are immutable by default; a change makes a new value.
Clock, randomness, identifiers and the environment are reached through ports, never called directly from the logic.
One place reads the environment: `root/`, or the configuration provider a lower block names.
Asynchronous work is awaited, or detached on purpose with its failure handled.
Every call across a process boundary has a timeout and can be cancelled.
Concurrent work is started within a scope that waits for it, cancels it, and receives its failures; no task outlives the operation that started it.
A fast source — a resize, a scroll, a stream — updates state at most once per frame, folding its events in batches.

An operation that may be repeated is idempotent: a key is minted once per intent and sent with every attempt, child identifiers are derived deterministically, and a transition to the current state does nothing.

A pattern answers a present problem, and then the canonical one: strategy plus registry for vendors and kinds, factory or module object for adapters, decorator at the composition root, reducer for transitions, transition table for state machines, builder for test data.
Behaviour is composed from small units.
Don't-repeat-yourself applies to knowledge, not to text that merely looks alike.
A function either answers a question or changes state, never both.
A unit calls its own collaborators, never the collaborators of their collaborators: no chain that walks into another object's internals.
A spec proves one boundary and is named after it.
A constant gets a spec only when a reader outside the code relies on it — a code users script against, a name another system reads — and then as one table per contract.
A case checks an outcome a caller observes — a returned value, a changed state, what a user sees — and a call on a fake only when the call itself is the behaviour.
A case earns its place by failing for a plausible bug no other case catches.
A case proves one intent and asserts it with strict equality on the whole outcome.
Variants of one behaviour are one table of cases, each row naming its condition.
No snapshot of a structure a reader cannot check by eye.
Every failure a boundary declares has a case that produces it and checks what the caller receives.
Edge cases are chosen by risk: empty input, limits, Unicode, invalid input, a concurrent call, a lost connection.
An invariant is proven by a property test where one pays — a value object's guard, an invertible mapper, a reducer — with its cases in the spec of its unit.
A lifecycle test takes an object made by its factory through every transition to its final state, and checks each step.
Each port has one contract suite, run against its fake and against its real adapter.
Tests ship in the same change as the behaviour they prove.
Every test has been seen failing for the right reason: written before the code, or after it with the code broken for a moment.
A bug fix begins with the test that reproduces the bug, seen failing before the fix.
When a behaviour is described before it is built — in an issue or a plan — an agent writes its tests from the description first.
Tests touch no network, no real file system outside a temporary folder, no real clock, no process they did not start and no credential.
Network, time, randomness, processes and credentials are faked through their ports, with one fake per port, named `<port>.fake`.
Each adapter is proven against its real engine inside the sandbox, in `<name>.integration.spec`, with a case for each port operation and each failure it maps.
Each critical scenario `PROJECT.md` names has one end-to-end test through the delivery layer, in `<name>.e2e.spec`.

A file in `__tests__/`, or in the folder of end-to-end specs, is a spec named after the file or scenario it proves — `<name>.spec`, `<name>.integration.spec`, `<name>.e2e.spec` — a fake `<port>.fake`, or fixtures `<name>.fixtures`, and nothing else; the language fixes the spelling.
Production code never imports a file of `__tests__/` or of the end-to-end folder.
A suite is named after its boundary, and a case reads `should <behaviour> when <condition>`, in the language's spelling.
A case has three parts — Arrange, Act, Assert — each marked and present once, and Act makes one call.
No test is skipped, pending, focused or without an assertion.
The project's check runs the tests, and fails when one fails.

All logic — the domain, the adapters, the libraries, the UI — is held at 100 percent of lines and functions, and of branches where the runner measures them, reached only through the tests of its boundaries.
Mutation testing measures the tests, and every mutant of the logic is killed.
No secret is committed — not in code, documents, tests, fixtures or history.
A secret never travels in a URL, and never reaches a build artefact: an image layer, a client bundle, a variable baked in at build time.
A secret that leaked — into a commit, a log, a message — is rotated at once, and the access made with it while it was exposed is checked.
No secret and no personal data appear in logs, errors, test data or documents.
Every environment variable the program reads is declared in one place, and code reads only declared names.
A credential belongs to one identity and one purpose, per environment, with only the permissions its job needs, documented beside its use.
A language uses one package manager, and one lockfile, committed.
A third-party step of CI is pinned to an immutable reference, never to a moving tag or branch.
Dependency updates arrive as pull requests from an update bot, each passing the check before it is merged.
A new release of a dependency is adopted only after a cooldown of some days, except a fix for a known vulnerability.

A new dependency is a decision: it needs a reason it cannot be a few lines of the project's own, and it is checked against the risk signs of a new package — a name one typo from a popular one, younger than thirty days, under a hundred weekly downloads, a recent change of owner, no source repository, obfuscated code.
A dependency deprecated as a whole is replaced — by its successor, another package, or the project's own code.
A dependency's install scripts run only when the dependency is listed by name as allowed to run them.
A high or critical known vulnerability in any dependency, development dependencies included, fails the check.
Every dependency's licence is on the project's allowlist.
Commit hooks, linter configurations and release automation come from shared, pinned packages, not from copies in each repository.
An operation that destroys data, spends money, touches a live system or sends something outward runs only with an explicit flag and a person's go-ahead; its default is to show what it would do.
Access is denied unless a rule grants it.
Before a change, read the rules that govern it: core's chapters and the files of the active blocks whose concern the change touches.
A change does what the task asks and nothing else: no unrelated refactor, reformat or rename.
A file that moves is moved, never deleted and written anew, and a moved file is not rewritten in the same step.
One command runs every check of the repository — format, lint, types, tests, coverage, mutation, the rest of the project's tools — and `constitution.yaml` names it.
The check verifies and never changes a tracked file: it generates nothing, formats nothing and rewrites nothing.
The check passes, with no error and no warning, before a change is reported done.
Before a change is handed back, it is reviewed against every active rule that no tool holds, not only those the task seemed to touch.
A repository keeps at its root `constitution.yaml`, the blocks it follows and their overrides, and `PROJECT.md`, the product's context.
`README.md` says what the repository is, how to install and run it, and how to change it — for a reader who knows nothing else.
`docs/` is for readers outside the code: users, integrators, operators.
Specs, plans and working notes live in a `local/` folder that version control ignores.
Generated files are not committed; the build produces them.
Files and folders are named in kebab-case.
A public repository carries a licence file that names its author.
A rule is never broken silently.

An agent asks before: adding a dependency, a pattern or an abstraction; changing a public surface, a schema or a format; an operation that destroys, costs money, touches a live system or sends something outward; a call to a real external service; pushing to a shared branch.
A design question is settled in the chat before code is written for it.
When a request can be read in two ways that lead to different work, the agent asks.
Outcomes are reported as they are: a failing test with its output, a skipped step as skipped, a claim about the code checked against the code.
Only a person decides what is committed.
An agent never merges, never pushes to the main line, never force-pushes and never rewrites shared history.
Commits, pull requests and documents carry no attribution to the tool or model that helped write them.
An agent that delegates keeps the responsibility: it names the rules and files that govern the task, and checks what comes back before it relies on it.
A sub-agent does the work it is given and nothing more: it never commits, never pushes or merges, never runs a live system and never calls a real external service.
A project keeps no agent instruction file of its own that restates a rule; the constitution delivers the rules, and `PROJECT.md` the context.
What an agent learns about the product goes into `PROJECT.md` through a change a person reviews; an agent's private memory is never the project's fact.
One document the user writes is the program's single input; every run reads it whole, validates it, and moves the world toward it.
Each section of the document has a strict schema: unions selected by a discriminant field, unknown keys rejected, every constraint between fields checked in validation, never at the point of use.
A section may be absent, and is then left untouched.
A secret in the document is a reference by name to the environment.
Each kind of value — a size, a duration — has one syntax in the document, parsed once.
The schema published for editors is generated from the code's schema, never written by hand.
The document and its schema live in `composition/`, which knows every section.
An `init` command writes one document from a template, named after the program, pointing editors at the published schema.
Validate, render, plan and apply are separate use-cases: each runs alone, and later ones reuse earlier ones.
A pipeline use-case keeps its stages under `steps/`, in the order the use-case calls them; a stage never calls another.
The plan names every change that destroys something, and apply refuses one without an explicit flag.
Applying the same document twice reports no change the second time, and a test proves it.
A run reports each stage — skipped with its reason, unchanged, changed, ran, failed — as a value the delivery layer prints.
What a run produces lands in one work folder that version control ignores.
Engines the program drives are not vendored: each is downloaded per release into the program's home, pinned by version and checksum, and reached only through a port.
Developers and CI run exactly the engines the program installed, linked into one directory of its home.
The library offers strict objects that fail on an unknown key.
The library offers unions selected by a discriminant field, with an error that names it.
The library generates a JSON Schema from the code's schema.
A repository of packages keeps each package at `packages/<language>/libs/<name>/`, language-free files and hooks in `packages/common/`, and templates per language and in `common`.
The root of a repository of packages is private: it holds only the workspace, the scripts of the check, and a README with one row per package.
A package holds its manifest, its README, its licence, its `configs/` or `src/`, and its `__tests__/`.
A package is named `<scope>/<kit>-<language>-<name>`, after what it configures.
`common` imports nothing.
A package ships configuration, primitives or tooling, never a product's business, and knows nothing of those who install it.
The manifest lists every entry a consumer may use and nothing else, and names the files it ships.
The tool a package configures is a peer dependency with a lowest supported version, never a dependency of the package.
Consumers extend a package's entries; they never copy its files.
A file no tool can extend is a template: kept canonical under `templates/`, copied once, then owned by the consumer.

A consumer takes a package by the tool's own extends, else by a one-line module that re-exports it, else by the tool's remote configuration; it pins the package through its lockfile and updates it through the bot.
The root of a repository of packages installs its own packages and extends them as a consumer would.
A copy generated from `common` is rebuilt by the package's build, never edited by hand, and a spec asserts it equals its source.
Each shipped configuration has a spec that parses it and asserts its intent; code a package runs is held by the coverage gate like any other.
Every package ships its licence file.
A package's README shows the install line, the one-line extends and its options.
All packages of a repository share one version; two packages at different versions are an error.
Versions follow semantic versioning: major for a breaking change of an entry, shipped with its migration; minor for an addition; patch for a fix.
A deprecated entry names its replacement and the version that removes it.
One tag publishes every public package; a version already published is skipped, so a rerun is safe.
The registry trusts the release job's identity and records provenance; no stored token publishes.
The changelog of a release is the commit subjects since the previous tag, features and fixes first.
The root resolves its own packages from the working tree, not from the registry.
The tool publishes through a CI identity with provenance, without a stored token.
Every request over the network has a timeout and can be cancelled.
A timeout or a lost connection is an expected, typed failure the user sees and can retry, never a hang or a silent loss.
Input the user entered survives a failed request and is sent again without being typed again.
A request's timeout and its lost connection each have a test case.
Nothing shipped to the client — code, configuration, data in memory or in storage — is treated as hidden from its user.
No secret is in client code, a client bundle or a value built into it.
Every check on the client — validation, permission, limit, price — is repeated where the client cannot reach it.
A commit holds one logical change, and its subject says what changed.
A refactor and a change of behaviour are never one commit.
Every commit passes the repository's check: the commit hooks run its fast part, CI runs all of it.
The reason for a change is written down where the flow puts it, beside the change, not only in a conversation.
Every change reaches the main line through a reviewed pull request.
The main line is protected: no direct push, no force push, no deletion.
The check runs in CI on every pull request, and a red check blocks the merge.
A repository integrates by one strategy, which the protection enforces, and no work-in-progress or fix-up commit reaches the main line.
A pull request is small enough to review in one sitting; one that mixes concerns is split.
A branch is deleted once it is merged.
When work is handed back, the working copy holds no stray change and no scratch file outside ignored folders.
History others have is never rewritten.
A release is marked by a tag of its version on the commit it was built from, and a tag never moves.
Releases are cut by automation from the merged changes; a person promotes a pre-release to a release.
Large binary files live outside the history, stored by reference.
A secret that reached the history is compromised: it is rotated at once, and rewriting the history does not undo the leak.
The delivery layer is `cli/`: one `<name>.cli` file per command, shared flag definitions in files beside them, reused and never declared twice, and the list of commands registered beside the files.
A command parses its flags, resolves its input, calls one use-case or composition, and prints the result.
What a run reports is a value the command prints at the end, never lines the logic prints along the way.
Data goes to standard output; diagnostics and failures go to standard error.
A command that reports data prints it as JSON when given `--json`.
Exit codes come from one map: 0 success, 1 a failure the user can act on, 2 a usage error — an unknown command, a bad flag — and 70 an internal error, the program's own bug.
Every value the run knows to be secret is masked in all output, an engine's output included, before it is printed.
A setting given in several places takes the flag first, then the environment, then the file.
Without a terminal the program never prompts; a missing answer is a usage error that names its flag.
A command's spec runs the program on an argument list with a fake command context, and checks standard output, standard error and the exit code.
Flags are declared with a schema and parsed before the handler runs.
The program's handler decides every exit code, the framework's own failures included.
The framework's terminal, prompts, clock and process hooks can be replaced in a spec.
An import that leaves its module uses `#/`; files inside one module import each other by relative path.
`#/` resolves only through `imports` in `package.json` (`"#/*": "./src/*"`).
Source files are kebab-case `.ts`, and `.tsx` only where markup is written.
A file with one export is named after it — `order-status.ts` exports `OrderStatus`; a file with several exports names the unit they form.
PascalCase for types, classes, enums and their members; camelCase for functions, variables and instances; SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for a constant value, camelCase for a constant object or function.
A type is a noun, undecorated: no `I` prefix, on ports too, and no `Type` or `Interface` suffix.
A group of named values is a string `enum`.
Internal code spells absence as `undefined`: `?: T` for what may be absent, `T | undefined` only where an explicit `undefined` means something, `return;` for no result.
Comparisons are strict — `===` and `!==`, with `null` too; never `==`.
`??` gives a default and `?.` reaches through an absent value; `!value` is never a check for absence on a value that is not boolean.
No `any`: not `: any`, `as any`, `Record<string, any>` or `Promise<any>`, in tests too; `noImplicitAny` is never turned off.
No `as` cast except `as const`, no `!` non-null assertion, no `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-nocheck`.
A value from beyond the boundary — `JSON.parse`, a response body, a file, a message — is `unknown` until a schema parses it.
A branch over a union handles every member: a `switch` whose default proves `never`, or an `if` chain that ends in a `never` check.
Conformance to a type is checked with `satisfies`, which keeps the narrow type, not with `as` or a widening annotation.
An identifier's brand is `string & { readonly __brand: 'OrderId' }` or a unique symbol, set only in the mapper at the boundary.

A project may declare semantic aliases — `type Email = string` — in one ambient `types.d.ts` at its source root: only aliases it uses, each for a meaning found in two or more places, never for a string that is just a string.
A type derivable from an exported parent in one or two indexed accesses is derived where it is used, not exported under a name of its own.
Arguments past the first travel in one options object, typed by an interface named `<Function>Input`.
JSDoc documents only a public API whose use is not obvious, never a self-describing property or parameter.

The compiler, not a bundler or the runtime, is the type gate: `tsc --noEmit` runs in the check with the strict options — `strict`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters`, `noImplicitOverride`, `noImplicitReturns`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`.
Build, test and lint tools are development dependencies, and production code imports none of them.
Each dependency has one version across every manifest of the repository.
A manifest's ranges are caret ranges; the lockfile pins the exact versions.
A package that holds state or types across the program — the schema engine, the interface framework — resolves to one version in the lockfile.
The fields of `package.json` follow the shared order.
`exports` in `package.json` maps each entry to its file, with a `types` condition beside `default` wherever a consumer imports code; `files` lists exactly what ships.
The tool a package configures is a `peerDependencies` entry with a `>=` floor.
